question:
According to Dicey, which of the following is NOT one of the three components of the Rule of Law?
(A) Absence of arbitrary power
(B) Equality before law
(C) Primacy of individual rights enforced by regular courts
(D) Separation of powers between legislature, executive and judiciary
answer:
D
Separation of powers is not part of Dicey's trinity; it is a separate principle associated with Montesquieu. Dicey's components are absence of arbitrary power, equality before law, and primacy of individual rights enforced by regular courts.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Dicey_Rule_of_Law Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::54 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which scholar is most closely associated with the formulation of the Rule of Law that influenced the Indian Constitution?
(A) A.V. Dicey
(B) Montesquieu
(C) John Locke
(D) Jean-Jacques Rousseau
answer:
A
A.V. Dicey's concept of Rule of Law (absence of arbitrary power, equality before law, primacy of individual rights) directly influenced the phrasing of Article 14. Montesquieu is associated with separation of powers, Locke with natural rights, Rousseau with social contract.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Dicey_Rule_of_Law Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::55 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The phrase 'equal protection of laws' in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution is borrowed from which source?
(A) British common law
(B) The 14th Amendment of the US Constitution
(C) The French Declaration of the Rights of Man
(D) The Irish Constitution of 1937
answer:
B
The phrase 'equal protection of laws' is directly derived from the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution. Article 14 also incorporates the British concept of 'equality before law' (from Dicey) but the specific phrase 'equal protection' is American.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Equal_Protection_US Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::56 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Part III of the Indian Constitution deals with:
(A) Directive Principles of State Policy
(B) Fundamental Rights
(C) Fundamental Duties
(D) Union and its Territory
answer:
B
Part III (Articles 12–35) contains the Fundamental Rights, which are justiciable. Part IV has Directive Principles, Part IV-A has Fundamental Duties, and Part I deals with Union and its Territory.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Fundamental_Rights_PartIII Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::57 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which traditional social hierarchy in India necessitated the prohibition of discrimination on grounds of caste in Article 15?
(A) Class system
(B) Caste system
(C) Tribal hierarchy
(D) Feudal system
answer:
B
The caste system (varna/jati) is the traditional social hierarchy that historically caused discrimination. Article 15 specifically prohibits discrimination on the ground of caste. Class system is economic, tribal hierarchy is not the primary target.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Caste_System Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::58 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Article 15 of the Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on which of the following grounds?
(A) Religion, race, caste, sex, and place of birth
(B) Religion, language, caste, and economic status
(C) Race, colour, sex, and property
(D) Caste, creed, gender, and domicile
answer:
A
Article 15(1) expressly lists: religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth. Language and economic status are not in this list; colour and property are not in Article 15 (they appear in other contexts like Article 14 or in other constitutions).
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Discrimination_Grounds_Article15 Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::59 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Universal adult franchise is the principle that every adult citizen has the right to vote. In the Indian Constitution, this principle is enshrined in:
(A) Article 19
(B) Article 326
(C) Article 325
(D) Article 21
answer:
B
Article 326 directly provides that elections to the Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies shall be on the basis of adult suffrage. Article 325 prohibits discrimination in electoral rolls. Article 19 deals with freedom of speech, Article 21 with right to life.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Universal_Adult_Franchise_Article326 Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::60 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Under the Indian Constitution, which legislative bodies are directly elected by the people on the basis of adult suffrage?
(A) Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
(B) Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies
(C) State Legislative Councils and Legislative Assemblies
(D) Only the Lok Sabha
answer:
B
According to Article 326, elections to the Lok Sabha and the Legislative Assembly of every State shall be on the basis of adult suffrage. Rajya Sabha is indirectly elected, Legislative Councils are also indirectly elected or partly nominated.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Directly_Elected_Bodies Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::61 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which part of the Indian Constitution?
(A) Part III
(B) Part IV
(C) Part IV-A
(D) Part II
answer:
B
Part IV (Articles 36–51) contains the Directive Principles of State Policy. Part III has Fundamental Rights, Part IV-A has Fundamental Duties, Part II deals with Citizenship.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::DPSP_PartIV Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::62 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution are listed in:
(A) Article 51-A
(B) Article 51
(C) Article 50
(D) Article 38
answer:
A
Article 51-A (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) lists the Fundamental Duties. Article 51 promotes international peace, Article 50 separates judiciary from executive, Article 38 is a Directive Principle for social justice.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Fundamental_Duties_Article51A Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::63 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Article 51-A(e) of the Indian Constitution makes it a duty of every citizen to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women. This duty is a response to which of the following?
(A) Colonial laws
(B) Historical and social practices derogatory to women
(C) International conventions
(D) Recommendations of the Law Commission
answer:
B
The fundamental duty to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women was added to address long-standing social practices like sati, child marriage, dowry, etc. While international conventions may have influenced, the primary context is indigenous social practices.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Practices_Derogatory_to_Women Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::64 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Federalism, as a system of government, is characterised by:
(A) A unitary central government with no regional units
(B) A division of powers between a central government and regional governments
(C) A confederation where states are sovereign
(D) A system where the central government can abolish states at will
answer:
B
Federalism involves a constitutional division of powers between two levels of government, each autonomous in its own sphere. Option A describes a unitary system, C a confederation, D is not typical of any known system (even in unitary systems, abolition is not at will without legal process).
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Federalism_Definition Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::65 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which of the following best distinguishes a 'Union of States' from a 'Federation' in the context of the Indian Constitution?
(A) In a Union, states have equal representation in the Upper House; in a Federation, they do not
(B) In a Union, states have no right to secede; in a Federation, they do
(C) In a Union, the centre has residuary powers; in a Federation, residuary powers belong to states
(D) In a Union, the constitution is written; in a Federation, it is unwritten
answer:
B
The key distinction made by Dr. Ambedkar is that a Union is indestructible; states cannot secede. In a federation (like the USA), there is no explicit right to secede either, but the term 'Union' was deliberately chosen to stress permanence. Option C is not always true (India has residuary powers with Centre, but so do some federations). Option A is not a defining feature.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Union_vs_Federation_Secession Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::66 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which member of the Constituent Assembly justified calling India a 'Union of States' by arguing that the states have no right to secede?
(A) Jawaharlal Nehru
(B) B.R. Ambedkar
(C) Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar
(D) K.M. Munshi
answer:
B
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee, explained in the Constituent Assembly that the term 'Union of States' was used to indicate that the Indian Union is indestructible and states have no right to secede. Nehru, Ayyar, and Munshi played other important roles.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Ambedkar_Union_of_States Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Foundation Inventory::67 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The term 'Preamble' in constitutional context refers to:
(A) The concluding part of the Constitution
(B) The introduction or preface to the Constitution
(C) The schedule listing the states
(D) The chapter on Fundamental Rights
answer:
B
The Preamble is the introductory statement that sets out the guiding principles and philosophy of the Constitution. It is not the conclusion, a schedule, or a chapter on rights.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Preamble_Definition Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::1 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The Preamble to the Indian Constitution is said to contain the:
(A) detailed provisions of the Constitution
(B) summary or essence of the Constitution
(C) list of fundamental duties
(D) procedure for constitutional amendments
answer:
B
The Preamble provides the essence and philosophy of the Constitution in a brief form. Detailed provisions are in the Articles, fundamental duties in Part IV-A, amendment procedure in Part XX.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Preamble_Essence Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::2 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The Preamble to the Indian Constitution is based on which document?
(A) The Government of India Act, 1935
(B) The Objectives Resolution
(C) The Nehru Report, 1928
(D) The US Declaration of Independence
answer:
B
The Preamble is explicitly based on the Objectives Resolution drafted and moved by Jawaharlal Nehru and adopted by the Constituent Assembly in 1947. The GoI Act 1935 was the previous constitutional framework, but not the source of the Preamble.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Preamble_Based_on_Objectives_Resolution Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::3 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Who drafted and moved the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly?
(A) B.R. Ambedkar
(B) Sardar Patel
(C) Jawaharlal Nehru
(D) Rajendra Prasad
answer:
C
Jawaharlal Nehru drafted and moved the Objectives Resolution on December 13, 1946. Ambedkar was Chairman of the Drafting Committee, Patel was a key leader, Rajendra Prasad was President of the Assembly.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Objectives_Resolution_Nehru Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::4 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The Objectives Resolution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on:
(A) December 13, 1946
(B) January 22, 1947
(C) November 26, 1949
(D) January 26, 1950
answer:
B
The Objectives Resolution was moved on December 13, 1946, and adopted on January 22, 1947. November 26, 1949 is when the Constitution was adopted, and January 26, 1950 is when it came into effect.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Objectives_Resolution_Adoption_Date Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::5 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The Constitution of India was adopted on:
(A) January 26, 1950
(B) November 26, 1949
(C) August 15, 1947
(D) January 22, 1947
answer:
B
The Constitution was adopted on November 26, 1949, as stated in the Preamble. It came into effect on January 26, 1950 (Republic Day). August 15, 1947 is Independence Day. January 22, 1947 is the adoption date of the Objectives Resolution.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Date_of_Adoption_Nov26_1949 Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::6 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which constitutional amendment added new words to the Preamble?
(A) 42nd Amendment, 1976
(B) 44th Amendment, 1978
(C) 73rd Amendment, 1992
(D) 86th Amendment, 2002
answer:
A
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 added the words Socialist, Secular, and Integrity to the Preamble. The 44th Amendment deleted the right to property from Fundamental Rights, 73rd dealt with Panchayats, 86th added right to education.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::42nd_Amendment_1976 Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::7 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which three words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment?
(A) Socialist, Secular, Integrity
(B) Socialist, Secular, Republic
(C) Sovereign, Socialist, Secular
(D) Socialist, Democratic, Integrity
answer:
A
The three words added were 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity'. 'Sovereign', 'Democratic', and 'Republic' were already present in the original Preamble.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Words_Added_42nd_Amendment Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::8 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
According to the text of the Preamble, the Constitution is adopted, enacted, and given to ourselves by:
(A) The Constituent Assembly
(B) We, the People of India
(C) The Parliament of India
(D) The President of India
answer:
B
The opening phrase 'We, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA... do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION' clearly states the people of India as the source of authority. The Constituent Assembly was the body that drafted it, but the authority flows from the people.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Text_of_Preamble_Source_of_Authority Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::9 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question: The source of authority of the Indian Constitution, as stated in the Preamble
is:
n(A) The Parliament of India
(B) The Constituent Assembly
(C) The people of India
(D) The President of India
answer:
C
The Preamble begins with 'We, the People of India', which establishes that the Constitution derives its authority from the people. The Constituent Assembly was the representative body that framed it, but ultimate sovereignty lies with the people.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Source_of_Authority_People Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::10 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which jurist called the Preamble the 'identity card of the Constitution'?
(A) K.M. Munshi
(B) N.A. Palkhivala
(C) M. Hidayatullah
(D) Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Iyer
answer:
B
N.A. Palkhivala, an eminent jurist and constitutional expert, described the Preamble as the 'identity card of the Constitution'. K.M. Munshi called it the 'horoscope', Hidayatullah said it resembles the US Declaration of Independence.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Palkhivala_Identity_Card Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::11 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Who described the Preamble as the 'horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'?
(A) Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava
(B) K.M. Munshi
(C) Sir Ernest Barker
(D) M. Hidayatullah
answer:
B
K.M. Munshi, a member of the Drafting Committee, called the Preamble the 'horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'. Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava called it the 'soul of the Constitution', Sir Ernest Barker called it the 'key-note'.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Munshi_Horoscope Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::12 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which member of the Constituent Assembly described the Preamble as the 'most precious part of the Constitution'?
(A) K.M. Munshi
(B) Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava
(C) Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Iyer
(D) Jawaharlal Nehru
answer:
B
Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava said the Preamble is 'the most precious part of the Constitution. It is the soul of the Constitution. It is a key to the Constitution.'
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Bhargava_Most_Precious_Part Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::13 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which of the following descriptions of the Preamble was given by Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava?
(A) Identity card of the Constitution
(B) Horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic
(C) Soul of the Constitution
(D) Key-note to the Constitution
answer:
C
Bhargava called the Preamble the 'soul of the Constitution'. N.A. Palkhivala called it 'identity card', K.M. Munshi called it 'horoscope', and Sir Ernest Barker called it 'key-note'.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Preamble_Soul_Bhargava Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::14 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The Preamble has been described as a 'key to the Constitution'. Who said this?
(A) K.M. Munshi
(B) N.A. Palkhivala
(C) Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava
(D) Sir Ernest Barker
answer:
C
Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava called the Preamble 'a key to the Constitution'. Sir Ernest Barker called it 'key-note' (note the different phrasing).
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Bhargava_Key_to_Constitution Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::15 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which metaphor did Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava use for the Preamble?
(A) 'A jewel set in the Constitution'
(B) 'The lamp of the Constitution'
(C) 'The foundation of the Constitution'
(D) 'The lighthouse of the Constitution'
answer:
A
Bhargava said 'It is a jewel set in the Constitution.' The other options are not recorded quotes from constitutional experts in this context.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Bhargava_Jewel_Set Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::16 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
According to Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava, the Preamble is a 'proper yardstick' to:
(A) measure the length of the Constitution
(B) measure the worth of the Constitution
(C) judge the validity of laws
(D) interpret the Fundamental Rights
answer:
B
Bhargava said the Preamble is 'a proper yardstick with which one can measure the worth of the Constitution'. It is not a tool for judicial review of laws (that's the basic structure doctrine).
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Bhargava_Yardstick Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::17 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which English political scientist described the Preamble as the 'key-note' to the Constitution?
(A) A.V. Dicey
(B) Sir Ernest Barker
(C) Sir Ivor Jennings
(D) Granville Austin
answer:
B
Sir Ernest Barker, author of 'Principles of Social and Political Theory', called the Preamble the 'key-note' to the Constitution. Dicey is known for Rule of Law, Jennings wrote about Indian Constitution, Austin wrote 'The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation'.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Barker_Key_Note Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::18 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Former Chief Justice M. Hidayatullah observed that the Preamble resembles:
(A) The French Declaration of the Rights of Man
(B) The Declaration of Independence of the United States
(C) The English Bill of Rights
(D) The Australian Commonwealth Act
answer:
B
M. Hidayatullah said the Preamble resembles the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. The ideals of liberty, equality, fraternity are from the French Revolution, but the structural resemblance is to the US Declaration.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Hidayatullah_US_Declaration Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::19 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
According to M. Hidayatullah, the Preamble is more than a declaration; it is:
(A) the source of all constitutional powers
(B) the soul of our Constitution that lays down the pattern of our political society
(C) a legally enforceable part of the Constitution
(D) a preface that can be ignored by the courts
answer:
B
Hidayatullah said the Preamble is 'the soul of our Constitution, which lays down the pattern of our political society'. It is not a source of power (A) and is non-justiciable (not enforceable in courts) (C and D are opposite).
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Hidayatullah_Soul_and_Pattern Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::20 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
What did M. Hidayatullah say about the alteration of the Preamble?
(A) It can be altered by a simple majority in Parliament
(B) It can be altered only with the consent of all states
(C) It contains a solemn resolve which nothing but a revolution can alter
(D) It cannot be altered under any circumstances
answer:
C
Hidayatullah said the Preamble 'contains a solemn resolve, which nothing but a revolution can alter'. However, the Supreme Court has held that the Preamble can be amended under Article 368, subject to the basic structure. Thus, the statement reflects its foundational importance, not legal amendability.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Hidayatullah_Revolution_Alter Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::21 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
In his concluding speech in the Constituent Assembly on November 25, 1949, Dr. Ambedkar stressed that political democracy cannot last unless it is based on:
(A) economic democracy
(B) social democracy
(C) industrial democracy
(D) direct democracy
answer:
B
Dr. Ambedkar said, 'Political democracy cannot last unless there lies at the base of it social democracy.' He defined social democracy as a way of life recognising liberty, equality and fraternity as a union.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Ambedkar_Social_Democracy Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::22 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
In 1997, the Supreme Court observed that the Constitution envisions to establish:
(A) a socialist state with nationalised industries
(B) an egalitarian social order rendering social, economic and political justice
(C) a theocratic state based on religious principles
(D) a confederation of states with strong regional autonomy
answer:
B
The Supreme Court in 1997 observed that the Constitution envisions to establish an egalitarian social order rendering to every citizen social, economic and political justice in a social and economic democracy. Option A is too specific (Indian socialism is democratic socialism, not full nationalisation).
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Supreme_Court_1997_Egalitarian_Social_Order Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::23 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Indian Preamble were borrowed from:
(A) The Russian Revolution (1917)
(B) The French Revolution (1789–1799)
(C) The American Revolution (1776)
(D) The British Magna Carta (1215)
answer:
B
The text explicitly states that the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity have been taken from the French Revolution (1789–1799). The idea of justice was taken from the Russian Revolution (1917).
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::French_Revolution_Ideals Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::24 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
The ideal of justice—social, economic and political—in the Preamble was derived from:
(A) The French Revolution
(B) The Russian Revolution
(C) The American Declaration of Independence
(D) The Irish Constitution
answer:
B
The text explicitly states that the ideal of justice—social, economic and political—has been taken from the Russian Revolution (1917). The French Revolution gave liberty, equality, fraternity.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Russian_Revolution_Justice Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::25 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which of the following correctly describes the justiciability of the Preamble?
(A) Its provisions are enforceable in courts of law
(B) It is non-justiciable, i.e., its provisions are not enforceable in courts
(C) It can be enforced only through writs
(D) It is justiciable only when read with Fundamental Rights
answer:
B
The Preamble is non-justiciable; its provisions cannot be enforced in courts of law. However, courts can use it as a guide for interpretation when the language of an article is ambiguous.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Preamble_Non_Justiciable Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::26 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
Which of the following is true regarding the Preamble's relation to legislative power?
(A) It is a source of power to the legislature
(B) It is a prohibition upon the powers of the legislature
(C) It is neither a source of power nor a prohibition upon legislative power
(D) It can be used to invalidate laws that contradict it
answer:
C
The Preamble is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a prohibition upon its powers. It is non-justiciable and cannot be used as a direct basis to invalidate laws, though it aids interpretation.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Preamble_Not_Source_Nor_Prohibition Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::27 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity

question:
On which date was the Objectives Resolution moved in the Constituent Assembly?
(A) December 13, 1946
(B) January 22, 1947
(C) November 26, 1949
(D) January 26, 1950
answer:
A
The Objectives Resolution was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on December 13, 1946. It was adopted on January 22, 1947.
tags: Chapter::Preamble2 Concept::Objectives_Resolution_Moved_Date Difficulty::Easy Type::Direct Level::Surface Inventory::28 Subject::Polity Book::Laxmikant
subject: Polity
